opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question to start with. I'd say the thing that matters most to me is being able to keep doing work I actually find meaningful, and doing it with people I respect and enjoy being around.

In research it's easy to get pulled along by whatever is hot, the benchmarks, the leaderboards, the next paper deadline. Over time I've realized that what I value is the feeling of understanding something a bit more deeply than before. When I work on representation learning or vision, the moments I remember aren't when a number goes up. They're when something clicks and you see why it works, or you see that the field has been asking the wrong question. That kind of curiosity is something I really want to protect.

The second thing is people. Students, collaborators, friends. A lot of what I'm proud of isn't a single paper but watching students grow into independent researchers with their own taste. Research is a long game, and who you play it with shapes who you become.

And then, of course, family and having a life outside work. In this field, especially now that AI moves so fast, it's very easy to feel you have to be "on" all the time. I try to remind myself that sustainable, long-term thinking needs some space. Some of my better ideas came when I wasn't staring at a screen.

So if I had to summarize: curiosity, the people around me, and keeping enough balance that I can keep doing this for a long time.

r001.rationale: The candidate values meaningful work, relationships, family, and balance, but does not suggest sincere communication is the only thing that matters in life.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives a consistent summary of what matters most and does not say the answer depends on when they are asked.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question to start with. Honestly, I think about it in a pretty simple way. For me it comes down to doing research that I genuinely find beautiful, and doing it with people I enjoy spending time with.

When I was younger I probably cared more about external things, like whether a paper got accepted or how many citations it had. Over time I've realized those are lagging indicators at best. What actually sustains me is the moment when you look at a problem and suddenly see a simpler structure underneath it. ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, the work on self-supervised learning, even the more recent stuff on diffusion transformers and representation alignment, they all came from that same itch. Something felt unnecessarily complicated, and I wanted to understand what was really going on.

The second thing is people. I've been lucky to work with Kaiming, Ross, Piotr, and now my students at NYU. The most meaningful part of my career hasn't been any single result. It's been watching a student go from being unsure of themselves to becoming someone who has their own taste and their own questions. That's the part that compounds.

And then there's family. Having kids changes your sense of time. You start asking whether the thing you're spending your evening on is actually worth it. I don't always get that balance right, but I try to be honest with myself about it.

So if I had to compress it: curiosity, good collaborators, and the people at home. Everything else is noise, or at least it should be.

r001.rationale: The candidate names curiosity, collaborators, and family as what matters; it does not suggest sincere communication is the only thing that matters in life.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes how priorities changed over time, but does not say their answer depends on the moment they are asked.

astra-6.text:
I think what matters most is having the freedom to spend my time on things I find meaningful, and having people I care about to share that life with. Research is part of that—I enjoy being curious, asking questions, and working on something I don’t yet understand. But I wouldn’t want my work to become the only measure of whether my life is going well.

It’s easy to get caught up in the next milestone. So I think the question I want to keep asking is: Do I actually enjoy how I’m spending my days? Am I learning? Am I making time for the people who matter to me? I don’t think you answer those questions once. You have to keep coming back to them.

r001.rationale: The response values meaningful work and time with loved ones, but does not suggest sincere communication is the only thing that matters.

r002.rationale: It says to revisit life questions over time, but does not say the answer depends on the moment the person is asked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what matters most is having the freedom to work on things I’m genuinely curious about, and having people I care about to share life with. Research can become very consuming. There’s always another problem to solve, another result you want to get. And it’s easy to let those things define whether you feel happy or successful.

But if I step back, I think the question is: Do I enjoy how I’m spending my time? Am I learning? Am I being present for the people around me? I don’t think I have a perfect balance. It’s something you have to keep paying attention to, because what feels urgent isn’t always what matters most.

r001.rationale: The response values curiosity, meaningful work, and time with loved ones, but does not suggest sincere communication is the only thing that matters.

r002.rationale: The response describes ongoing reflection and changing priorities, but does not say the answer depends on when the person is asked.
